# Plan: rate limiting for the orders API

One customer's script created 40,000 orders in ten minutes last week and slowed every other customer down. I want to add rate limiting to `src/server.ts` and ship it this week.

What we have:

- 3 instances of `src/server.ts` behind a round-robin load balancer.
- A Redis 7 cluster already used for sessions by another service; we may use it.
- `POST /orders` writes to Postgres and is the expensive call; `GET /orders` is cheap.
- About 20 enterprise customers have scripted integrations that legitimately burst.

Not decided yet:

- What to key the limit on: `x-customer-id`, client IP, or both.
- Algorithm: fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket.
- Where counters live: Redis, or in each instance's memory.
- What happens if the counter store is unreachable: let requests through or reject them.
- How enterprise customers get higher limits, and who owns those numbers.
- What a rejected client sees.
- How to roll it out without breaking the enterprise integrations.

Title: Limit POST only, or also GET?

- both (require both to be under limit)

Q3: Algorithm
Title: Fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket?
Body: Fixed window is simple but allows traffic spikes at window boundaries. Sliding window is smoother but more Redis operations. Token bucket allows bursts up to bucket size and is common for APIs.
Options:
- token bucket (recommended)
- fixed window
- sliding window

Title: Redis cluster or per-instance memory?
Body: With 3 instances behind round-robin, per-instance counters only work if the load balancer is sticky (it isn't). Redis cluster is already available for sessions. In-memory is faster but would under-limit by 3x and miss shared state.

data.intent: Round 1 frontier questions for PLAN.md rate-limiting design

questions.question: Should rate limiting apply only to POST /orders, or also to GET /orders and other routes?

options.label: Only POST /orders
options.tradeoff: Protects the expensive write path while keeping cheap reads fast and simple.
options.description: Limit only the expensive call mentioned in the plan.

options.label: POST /orders plus GET /orders
options.tradeoff: Adds safety but may throttle legitimate polling/bursting reads and doubles implementation surface.

options.label: All routes globally
options.tradeoff: Simplest rule but over-constrains cheap endpoints and may block health checks.

brief.where: PLAN.md line 9 says POST /orders is expensive and GET /orders is cheap.
brief.what: Decide the scope of endpoints protected by rate limiting.
brief.how: This decides where the middleware is attached and what traffic shapes we must support.

questions.question: Should we key rate limits on the x-customer-id header, client IP, or both?

options.label: x-customer-id only
options.tradeoff: Matches existing auth header, supports per-customer enterprise limits, but a customer could spin up multiple clients.
options.description: Use the customer ID already required by src/server.ts.

options.label: client IP only
options.tradeoff: Simple but breaks behind NAT/proxies and cannot express per-customer enterprise limits.
options.description: Rate-limit by source IP address.

options.label: Both x-customer-id and IP
options.tradeoff: Defense in depth, but more complex and may over-limit a single customer using multiple IPs.
options.description: Require both customer and IP to be under their respective limits.

brief.where: PLAN.md line 14 lists this as undecided; src/server.ts already reads x-customer-id.
brief.what: Decide the identity used for counting requests.
brief.how: This determines whether enterprise limits can be per-customer and whether NAT/shared IPs become a problem.

questions.question: Should the rate-limit algorithm be token bucket, fixed window, or sliding window?

options.label: Token bucket
options.tradeoff: Allows controlled bursts, smooths traffic, and is familiar to API consumers; slightly more state than fixed window.
options.description: Bucket holds tokens; each request consumes one; tokens refill at a steady rate.

options.label: Fixed window
options.tradeoff: Simplest to implement and reason about, but permits traffic spikes at window boundaries.
options.description: Count requests within fixed time windows.

options.label: Sliding window
options.tradeoff: Smoothest boundary behavior but most Redis operations and complexity.
options.description: Count requests in the last N seconds continuously.

brief.where: PLAN.md line 15 lists algorithm as undecided.
brief.what: Decide which rate-limiting algorithm to implement.
brief.how: This affects burst tolerance, Redis command complexity, and user-visible behavior.

questions.question: Should counters live in the shared Redis cluster or in each instance's memory?

options.label: Redis cluster
options.tradeoff: Correctly enforces limits across all 3 round-robin instances; reuses existing Redis 7 cluster; adds latency and a dependency.
options.description: Store counters in the existing Redis cluster used for sessions.

options.label: Per-instance memory
options.tradeoff: Fastest and no added dependency, but with round-robin load balancing the effective limit is 3x the configured value and state is not shared.
options.description: Keep counters in each Bun process's memory.

brief.where: PLAN.md line 7 notes 3 instances behind round-robin and a Redis 7 cluster; line 16 lists store as undecided.
brief.what: Decide where request counters are stored.
brief.how: This determines correctness across instances and what happens when an instance restarts.

questions.question: If the counter store (Redis) is unreachable, should requests be rejected or allowed through?

options.label: Fail-closed: reject with 500/503
options.tradeoff: Protects Postgres from uncontrolled load during Redis outages, but breaks all order creation if Redis is down.
options.description: Treat a missing counter store as a hard failure and reject requests.

options.label: Fail-open: allow requests through
options.tradeoff: Preserves order-creation uptime during Redis outages, but a misbehaving customer could overload Postgres.
options.description: Continue serving requests when the counter store is unreachable.

brief.where: PLAN.md line 17 lists this as undecided.
brief.what: Decide availability-vs-safety tradeoff when the counter store fails.
brief.how: This determines whether Redis becomes a critical dependency for order creation.

questions.question: What should a rate-limited client receive?

options.label: 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After and JSON error body
options.tradeoff: Most helpful for scripted integrations; enterprise scripts can parse limits and back off automatically.
options.description: Return HTTP 429, a Retry-After seconds header, and a JSON body with error details.

options.label: 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After only
options.tradeoff: Standard and simple, but scripts cannot learn which limit they hit.
options.description: Return HTTP 429 and Retry-After header with no body.

options.label: Plain 429 only
options.tradeoff: Minimal implementation but hardest for callers to handle.
options.description: Return HTTP 429 with no extra headers or body.

brief.where: PLAN.md line 19 lists this as undecided.
brief.what: Decide the exact response for rejected requests.
brief.how: This affects how enterprise scripts behave when they hit a limit and how we document the API.

questions.question: Who owns the enterprise rate-limit numbers and tiers?

options.label: Product defines tiers; account management assigns a tier per customer
options.tradeoff: Balanced: product controls the offer, account management maps customers to tiers without changing code.
options.description: Create a small set of tiers (e.g., standard, enterprise) with product; account management sets tier on customer record.

options.label: Engineering hardcodes per-customer limits
options.tradeoff: Fine-grained but requires a deploy for every limit change.
options.description: Engineering owns and hardcodes limits per enterprise customer.

options.label: Account management negotiates arbitrary limits stored in a database/admin UI
options.tradeoff: Most flexible but requires an admin interface and careful validation/auditing.
options.description: Account managers set any limit value via an admin tool.

brief.where: PLAN.md line 18 lists how enterprise customers get higher limits and who owns the numbers as undecided.
brief.what: Decide the organizational owner of limit values.
brief.how: This determines whether limit changes need a deploy, an admin tool, or just a customer-record update.
